nameStory: Milk parsley gets its name from the thin, milky white sap that oozes from its stems and leaves when broken - though this "milk" has a rather unpleasant, fetid smell that's nothing like cow's milk! The "parsley" part comes from its membership in the same plant family as garden parsley, sharing those characteristic umbrella-shaped flower clusters. Despite the name, this wild plant is definitely not something you'd want to sprinkle on your pasta!
description: Milk parsley is a tall, graceful wetland plant that can reach 3-5 feet high, with delicate, finely-divided leaves that look almost feathery. It belongs to the carrot family, so it has those distinctive flat-topped clusters of tiny white flowers arranged like little umbrellas. This is a biennial plant, meaning it takes two years to complete its life cycle - growing leaves the first year, then flowering and setting seed the second year before dying. You'll find it standing in shallow water or very wet soil, often with its feet literally in the marsh.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Hollow stems that are often tinged with purple, especially toward the base. When broken, they release a thin, foul-smelling milky sap that sticks to your fingers.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers arranged in large, flat-topped umbrella clusters (umbels) that can be 4-6 inches across. Each flower cluster looks like a delicate white doily against the green foliage.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Finely divided, feathery leaves with narrow, pointed segments that feel soft and delicate to the touch. The leaf segments have pinnatifid lobes - meaning they're deeply cut but not completely separated.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Flattened, oval seeds with three ridges on the back that are NOT winged (this helps distinguish it from similar species). Seeds develop in late summer after the flowers fade.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall and upright, often growing in small colonies in wet areas. Plants frequently stand right in shallow water or boggy soil where your boots would get soaked.

habitat: Look for milk parsley in New England's wetlands, especially along the shallow edges of rivers, ponds, and estuaries where the water level fluctuates seasonally. It thrives in marshes, wet ditches, and boggy areas that flood in spring but may dry out partially in summer. This plant can tolerate some shade, so you might find it growing under the dappled light of wetland trees and shrubs.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge from wet soil, showing their characteristic feathery foliage. This is when the milky sap is most abundant and noticeable if you break a stem.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time, with large white umbrella-shaped flower clusters creating a delicate display over the marsh. The purple-tinged hollow stems are most obvious now.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and flat, ridged seeds develop and ripen. Plants begin to turn yellow and brown as they complete their two-year life cycle.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back completely, leaving only seeds to start the cycle again. Look for dried, hollow brown stems poking up through ice or snow in wetland areas.

funFact: In parts of Europe and Russia, people have traditionally used milk parsley roots as a substitute for ginger in cooking - quite remarkable considering this humble marsh plant can provide the same warming spice as tropical ginger root!
confusionNotes: Milk parsley is easily confused with Cambridge milk parsley (Selinum carvifolia), which grows in similar wet places. The key difference: milk parsley has hollow, often purple-tinged stems and stinky milky sap, while Cambridge milk parsley has solid, green stems. Memory trick: "Hollow and purple, that's milk parsley!"
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you - milk parsley is completely unrelated to garden parsley and shouldn't be eaten! The "milk" is actually a latex sap that smells terrible and could be harmful. Also, be aware that "Cambridge milk parsley" is actually a different plant entirely (Selinum carvifolia), despite the similar common name - a perfect example of why botanists prefer scientific names!
compareHints: Milk parsley is the only member of the Peucedanum genus commonly found in New England wetlands. Its closest relatives in the carrot family include Cambridge milk parsley (Selinum carvifolia), but milk parsley's hollow, purple-tinged stems and foul-smelling milky sap make it distinctive. Unlike many other carrot family members that prefer drier ground, milk parsley specifically needs wet feet to thrive.
